title: The Medicine Chest and the Rope: Treaty 6 at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt
subtitle: Treaty No. 6 between the Crown and the nēhiyawak (Plains and Woods Cree), Nakoda and Saulteaux, Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt, 1876; Big Bear's adhesion, 1882
intro: In August 1876 the nēhiyawak (Plains Cree), with Nakoda (Assiniboine), Saulteaux and Woods Cree bands, met the Crown's commissioners at Fort Carlton, the old Hudson's Bay post on the North Saskatchewan. Lieutenant Governor Alexander Morris had brought the terms already accepted in Treaties 1 to 5: reserves, a cash present, small annuities, tools and schools. The Cree had asked for a treaty for years, Sweet Grass as early as 1871. They came to it as the buffalo were failing.

Between 18 and 23 August the Carlton councils turned on a single question: what would happen to the people while they learned to farm, and if famine came? Pītikwahanapiwīyin (Poundmaker) asked how the offer could feed and clothe his children; Ahtahkakoop asked for food in the planting seasons; Mistawāsis narrowed it to help at the start and in famine. Morris refused daily rations but granted more cattle and implements, three years of seed-time provisions, aid in a general famine or pestilence, and a medicine chest at each agent's house. None of these was in the earlier numbered treaties. Kamīyistowesit (Beardy) signed separately at Duck Lake on 28 August; Wīhkasko-kisēyin (Sweet Grass) signed first at Fort Pitt on 9 September. Mistahi-maskwa (Big Bear) arrived after the signing, would not sign, and asked to be spared the rope about his neck. He held out until hunger brought him to an adhesion at Fort Walsh on 8 December 1882.

The record is lopsided, and this chapter says so plainly. Almost everything is the Crown's: Morris's book of 1880, which prints his own report and the day-by-day narrative of his secretary A. G. Jackes, and the treaty text. Every Cree speech here was spoken in Cree, rendered into English by the commission's interpreters or by Peter Erasmus, the Cree-Métis interpreter the chiefs hired themselves, and condensed by Jackes. Quoted lines are labelled 'as interpreted'. Erasmus's memoir, dictated about 1920 and published in 1976, gives the view from inside the chiefs' council, including Poundmaker's line about pemmican that the official record omits. There are no diaries kept on the treaty ground.

The nations' own understanding comes down as oral history. Treaty 6 Elders interviewed in 1976 and in the 1990s described a land shared to the depth of a plough, not surrendered, and a medicine chest that meant doctors, medicines and hospitals. The written text records a surrender of land and a chest kept at the agent's direction. These are set side by side here as positions. The courts have also read the clause: Dreaver v. The King (1935) held that medicines must be supplied free; the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal read it narrowly in R. v. Johnston (1966) and R. v. Swimmer (1970); in Wuskwi Sipihk Cree Nation v. Canada (1999) the Federal Court said it may well require a full range of modern medical services.

The epilogue runs through the six years Big Bear refused, and through the Saskatchewan Herald, founded at Battleford in 1878, whose editorials called the treaty a contract to farm. Poundmaker and Big Bear were both imprisoned after 1885; Canada exonerated Poundmaker on 23 May 2019. In August 2026, for the 150th anniversary, the manuscript treaty went back inside the walls of Fort Carlton.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Morris and Jackes date the Carlton councils 18–23 August 1876 (arrival 15 August, Duck Lake signing 28 August) and the Fort Pitt councils 7–9 September, with Big Bear's speech on 13 September. Erasmus's memoir rarely gives days, so his entries carry approximate dates set by the adjournments in Jackes's narrative. The Elders' testimony is dated by the year it was recorded, not the year it describes.

eyes.name: Alexander Morris
eyes.role: Lieutenant Governor of Manitoba and the North-West Territories, aged 50; senior treaty commissioner (he had already concluded Treaties 3, 4 and 5)
eyes.where: Fort Garry, then the treaty grounds at Fort Carlton, Duck Lake and Fort Pitt

waypoints.label: Back at Fort Garry, 6 Oct; report 4 Dec

eyes.vantage_label: Crown commissioner who made the offer
eyes.form: speeches (in the secretary's narrative); official report; printed book (1880)
eyes.authenticity: His speeches survive in A. G. Jackes's narrative and his own dispatch of 4 December 1876 to the Minister of the Interior, both printed in his 1880 book. The book is a government man's compilation; it renders every Cree speech through the commission's interpreters.
eyes.bio: A Montreal-trained lawyer and former Ontario politician, Morris believed the treaties were the Crown's peaceful answer to the coming of settlement and the end of the buffalo. At Carlton he pressed for a quick, uniform agreement, refused daily rations, and gave way on cattle, implements, a medicine chest and a famine clause. His 1880 book, published to explain and defend the treaties, is the main written record of the councils.

sources.title: Alexander Morris, The Treaties of Canada with the Indians of Manitoba and the North-West Territories (1880), Project Gutenberg #7126
Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)

eyes.name: A. G. Jackes
eyes.role: Physician (M.D.) travelling as secretary to the commission; kept the day-by-day narrative of the councils
eyes.where: In the council tent at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt
eyes.authenticity: Printed as 'Narrative of the proceedings' in Morris (1880). It is a dated narrative rather than a verbatim minute: speeches are condensed, often in reported speech, and every Cree speaker comes through an interpreter's English.
eyes.bio: Jackes's narrative is the closest thing to minutes the councils have. It records ceremony, adjournments and Sunday services as well as speeches, and it preserves the chiefs' objections and requests that the written treaty partly absorbed. Because it is the commission's own record, what it leaves out matters as much as what it keeps.

sources.title: Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)
Jackes's narrative for 22–23 August (AccessGenealogy transcription of Morris)

eyes.name: William Joseph Christie
eyes.role: Retired Hudson's Bay Company chief factor, aged about 52; treaty commissioner responsible for payments and accounts
eyes.side: Canada (the Crown); long HBC service in the Saskatchewan country
eyes.where: Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt pay tables
eyes.form: pay lists and accounts (in Morris's report)
eyes.authenticity: His figures for the people paid and the money spent are reported in Morris (1880); his own pay lists are government records.
eyes.bio: Christie had run Fort Edmonton and the Saskatchewan district for the Company and was known to many of the chiefs before he sat as a commissioner. His work was the counting: chiefs, headmen, men, women and children paid, and the money returned unspent. His numbers give the councils their human scale.

sources.title: Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)

eyes.name: James McKay
eyes.role: Métis Manitoba politician and former HBC guide, fluent in Cree; treaty commissioner
eyes.side: Canada (the Crown); Métis of Red River
eyes.where: Fort Carlton; his own camp near Duck Lake

waypoints.label: Duck Lake meeting at his camp, 28 Aug

eyes.authenticity: His words survive only in Jackes's narrative in Morris (1880).
eyes.bio: McKay could address the chiefs in their own language, and Jackes records him speaking bluntly in the hardest session, on 22 August. He had travelled ahead of Morris and met Beardy before the council; the Duck Lake band's own signing took place at his camp. He died three years later.

sources.title: Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)
Jackes's narrative, 22 August (AccessGenealogy)

eyes.name: Peter Erasmus
eyes.role: Cree-Métis interpreter and former guide, aged 43, hired by Mistawasis and Ahtahkakoop as their own interpreter
eyes.side: Interpreter chosen by the nēhiyawak chiefs; later also paid by the commission
eyes.where: Fort Carlton council and the chiefs' private councils; Fort Pitt
eyes.authenticity: He dictated his life story at about 87 to the Métis journalist Henry Thompson; the typescript stops at 1885 and was published by the Glenbow-Alberta Institute in 1976 as 'Buffalo Days and Nights'. Written more than forty years after the event by a man who supported the treaty; post-1928, so digests only. Jackes's contemporary narrative confirms that he read out the chiefs' requests on 23 August.
eyes.bio: Erasmus is the only eyewitness who sat in the chiefs' own deliberations as well as the public council. He records Poundmaker and The Badger opposing the treaty and Mistawasis and Ahtahkakoop winning the argument, and he judged the commission's own interpreters inadequate. His later work for the commission exposed him to charges of divided loyalty.

sources.title: Michael Payne, 'Erasmus, Peter', Dictionary of Canadian Biography
Michael Cottrell, 'Erasmus, Peter (1833–1931)', Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan

eyes.name: Mistawāsis (Big Child)
eyes.role: Head chief of the House people among the nēhiyawak (Plains Cree) near Carlton, in his sixties

waypoints.label: Reserve west of Carlton (later Mistawasis First Nation)

eyes.vantage_label: head chief who argued for the treaty
eyes.authenticity: His words survive as the commission's interpreters rendered them, condensed by Jackes in Morris (1880), and in Erasmus's much later memoir. In 1875 George McDougall reported his words of welcome.
eyes.bio: Mistawāsis welcomed the promise of a treaty when George McDougall brought word of it in 1875. At Carlton he was the senior voice for acceptance, pressing for help in settling and in famine rather than daily food. Erasmus credits his speech in the chiefs' council with carrying the doubters.

sources.title: Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)
Michelle Filice, 'Treaty 6', The Canadian Encyclopedia (11 Oct 2016)

eyes.name: Ahtahkakoop (Star Blanket)
eyes.role: Chief of a nēhiyawak (Plains Cree) band near Sandy Lake, about 60; ally of Mistawāsis
eyes.authenticity: Known through Jackes's narrative in Morris (1880), which spells him Ah-tuk-ah-coop, and Erasmus's memoir.
eyes.bio: Ahtahkakoop's band already had houses, gardens, a church (1874) and a mission school opened in 1876. At Carlton he asked for food in the spring planting seasons and led the show of hands that ratified the terms. He signed beside Mistawāsis on 23 August.

sources.title: Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)
Ahtahkakoop First Nation (Indigenous Saskatchewan Encyclopedia, University of Saskatchewan)

eyes.name: Pītikwahanapiwīyin (Poundmaker)
eyes.role: Councillor under Red Pheasant among the River people of the nēhiyawak (Plains Cree), about 34; not yet a chief
eyes.form: speeches (as interpreted); words reported in a later memoir
eyes.authenticity: Jackes (in Morris 1880) gives his requests for help in settling. His best-known line, that the land was not a piece of pemmican to be cut up and handed back, comes from Erasmus's memoir (published 1976), not from the commission's record.
eyes.bio: Poundmaker spoke for those who doubted that the offer could feed and clothe their children once the buffalo were gone. He signed on 23 August. Convicted of treason after 1885, he died in 1886; on 23 May 2019 the Government of Canada formally exonerated him.

sources.title: Hugh A. Dempsey, 'Pītikwahanapiwīyin', Dictionary of Canadian Biography
CIRNAC, 'Looking back: brief history of Chief Poundmaker' (23 May 2019)

eyes.name: Kamīyistowesit (Beardy)
eyes.role: Chief of the Willow Cree (nēhiyawak) at Duck Lake, about 48
eyes.where: Duck Lake, refusing the Carlton camp
eyes.vantage_label: chief who would not come to Carlton
eyes.authenticity: His 28 August speech survives in Jackes's narrative in Morris (1880). His later protests (to Laird, 1877; to Dufferin, January 1878; to Lorne, 1881) are summarised in his DCB entry.
eyes.bio: Beardy would not come to the main council because the commissioners would not hold it where his vision directed; a separate meeting was held near Duck Lake. He asked for protection of the remaining buffalo and wanted his requests written down, then signed because he saw no other course. His band was suspended from treaty after 1885.

sources.title: John L. Tobias, 'Kamīyistowesit', Dictionary of Canadian Biography
Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)

eyes.name: Wīhkasko-kisēyin (Sweet Grass)
eyes.role: Principal chief of the nēhiyawak (Plains Cree) of the Fort Pitt country; baptised Abraham by Father Lacombe in 1870
eyes.form: speeches (as interpreted); message to the governor (1871)
eyes.authenticity: His 1871 message to Lieutenant Governor Archibald and his Fort Pitt speeches are printed in Morris (1880) as interpreted. He died in an accidental shooting about four months after signing.
eyes.bio: Sweet Grass had asked for a treaty as early as 1871, telling Archibald the fur animals were failing and his people needed help. At Fort Pitt he was the first to sign, speaking of peace and of red and white standing together. His death in January 1877 removed the strongest voice for the treaty in the western camps.

sources.title: Allan R. Turner, 'Wikaskokiseyin', Dictionary of Canadian Biography
Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)

eyes.name: Mistahi-maskwa (Big Bear)
eyes.role: Chief of a nēhiyawak (Plains Cree) band of the Fort Pitt country, about 50; spoke for camps still hunting on the plains
eyes.where: Arrived at Fort Pitt after the signing; later the Cypress Hills and Fort Walsh
eyes.form: speeches (as interpreted); words reported by a missionary
eyes.authenticity: His 1875 words come from George McDougall's report and his 1876 speech from Jackes's narrative, both in Morris (1880). The meaning of the 'rope' phrase is debated: Morris took it literally, as fear of hanging; Rudy Wiebe's DCB entry (1982) reads it also as a metaphor for lost freedom.
eyes.bio: Big Bear was the first major prairie chief to refuse Treaty 6, holding out for six years while the buffalo lasted and drawing independent hunters to his camp. Hunger brought him to sign an adhesion at Fort Walsh on 8 December 1882. After 1885 he was convicted of treason and imprisoned; he died in January 1888.

sources.title: Rudy Wiebe, 'Mistahimaskwa', Dictionary of Canadian Biography (1982)
Morris (1880), Chapter IX: The Treaties at Forts Carlton and Pitt (Confederation Debates, University of Victoria)

eyes.name: George Millward McDougall
eyes.role: Wesleyan Methodist missionary at Morleyville, aged 54; sent by Morris in 1875 to tell the Cree camps a treaty was coming
eyes.side: Canada (messenger for the Crown); Methodist mission
eyes.where: Travelling the Cree camps from Carlton to the Battle and Red Deer rivers

waypoints.label: Camps on the Battle and Red Deer rivers

eyes.vantage_label: messenger a year before the council
eyes.authenticity: His report to Morris, dated 23 October 1875, is printed in Morris (1880). He died in a blizzard in January 1876, before the council. (His son John McDougall's later books are not used here.)
eyes.bio: McDougall carried the Crown's message to the camps and wrote down how each received it. He reported Mistawāsis's welcome and Big Bear's suspicion, and his description of Big Bear as a troublemaker shaped how the commission saw him. His report is the prelude in the government's own record.

sources.title: Morris (1880): McDougall's report of 23 October 1875 (AccessGenealogy transcription)

eyes.name: Saskatchewan Herald (Patrick Gammie Laurie, editor)
eyes.role: First newspaper of the North-West Territories, published at Battleford by its founder-editor
eyes.where: Battleford, territorial capital, between Carlton and Fort Pitt
eyes.vantage_label: settler newspaper in the treaty country
eyes.authenticity: Issues are held by the Provincial Archives of Saskatchewan. The dated items here are known through W. H. Hildebrandt's 1978 MA thesis on Laurie, not read directly. Its editorials were often slanted against Indigenous and Métis people.
eyes.bio: Laurie hauled his press to Battleford to boost settlement, and his paper watched the treaty's aftermath from the settlers' side: rations, reserves, and Big Bear's refusals. Its editorials argued the treaty bound the nations to farm and blamed them for hunger. It is the voice the treaty's critics were answering.

sources.title: Canadian Typography archive: Saskatchewan Herald, 1878
Walter H. Hildebrandt, 'P.G. Laurie: The Aspirations of a Western Enthusiast' (MA thesis, University of Saskatchewan, 1978)

eyes.name: Treaty 6 Elders and Nations (published testimony and positions)
eyes.role: Elders of Treaty 6 First Nations interviewed in Alberta (1976) and Saskatchewan (1990s, published 2000), and the nations' later public positions
eyes.side: Treaty 6 First Nations (nēhiyawak, Nakoda, Dene, Saulteaux)
eyes.where: Treaty 6 communities in Alberta and Saskatchewan
eyes.language: Cree and other languages (published in English)
eyes.authenticity: Oral history handed down from the generation that made the treaty and recorded a century later: Lynn Hickey's 1976 interviews with Alberta Treaty 6 Elders and Harold Cardinal and Walter Hildebrandt, 'Treaty Elders of Saskatchewan' (2000). Cited here through Craft and Lebihan (NCCIH, 2021) and the Office of the Treaty Commissioner (2007). Modern publications: digests only.
eyes.bio: The Elders' accounts hold the spoken promises alongside the written text: a land to be shared, not sold, and a medicine chest meaning care for the people's health. They are positions held by the treaty nations and set beside the Crown's text without a verdict here.

sources.title: Aimée Craft and Alice Lebihan, The Treaty Right to Health: A Sacred Obligation (National Collaborating Centre for Indigenous Health, 2021)
Office of the Treaty Commissioner, Treaty Implementation: Fulfilling the Covenant (Saskatoon, 2007)

entries.place: Fort Edmonton country, message carried to Upper Fort Garry
entries.headline: Sweet Grass asks the new governor for a treaty
entries.digest: In the first years after Canada took over the Hudson's Bay Company lands, Sweet Grass sent word to Lieutenant Governor Archibald. The fur animals his people lived on were failing; he asked that men be sent to treat with the Cree and that the government give help. Morris later printed the message as part of the case that the Cree themselves wanted a treaty.
entries.source_note: DCB, Wikaskokiseyin (year only given); text printed in Morris (1880)

entries.place: A camp on the plains west of Carlton
entries.headline: Big Bear wants none of the Queen's presents
entries.digest: When McDougall read the governor's message, Big Bear tried to lead the council against it. He said the presents were bait: one scatters meat around a fox-trap, then knocks the fox on the head once it is caught. McDougall judged his party a small minority.
entries.quote: We want none of the Queen's presents (as interpreted)
entries.source_note: McDougall's report of 23 Oct 1875, in Morris (1880); month of the meeting not given

entries.headline: McDougall reports the camps ready to treat
entries.digest: McDougall wrote to Morris after visiting every camp he could reach, from Carlton to the Battle and Red Deer rivers, to read the governor's message. Mistawāsis, head chief at Carlton, received it gladly. McDougall described Big Bear as a troublesome man whose party was small, a view that travelled with the commission the following year.
entries.quote: That is just it, that is all we wanted (Mistawasis, as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Report dated 23 Oct 1875, in Morris (1880); AccessGenealogy transcription

entries.headline: Morris sets out with Christie and Jackes
entries.digest: Morris left Fort Garry with W. J. Christie and Dr Jackes, with James McKay to follow, on the long cart road west. The journey to the South Saskatchewan took nearly three weeks, by way of Fort Ellice, where they forded the Assiniboine on 4 August.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition): Morris's report of 4 Dec 1876

entries.headline: McKay meets Beardy before the council
entries.digest: McKay, travelling ahead, met Beardy of the Willow Cree and joined Morris on the road. The Duck Lake people would not come to the main camp at Carlton. This was the first sign that the nēhiyawak would not meet as one body on the commission's terms.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Arrival at Carlton after crossing the South Saskatchewan
entries.digest: On 14 August the party crossed the South Saskatchewan at Dumont's crossing, where Cree welcomed them. On the 15th Morris reached Fort Carlton, the old Hudson's Bay post on the North Saskatchewan, where the Cree lodges were already pitched.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Beardy keeps his people away from Carlton
entries.digest: Beardy refused to bring the Willow Cree to the Carlton camp. His biographer records that he wanted the council held where his vision directed, and the commissioners would not move it. The Carlton chiefs meanwhile asked for a day to confer among themselves.
entries.source_note: DCB, Kamīyistowesit; Morris (1880) for the 16–17 Aug delay

entries.headline: The chiefs hire their own interpreter
entries.digest: Mistawāsis and Ahtahkakoop engaged Erasmus to interpret for them, so that the Cree would hear the terms through a man they trusted. The commission's own interpreters, Peter Ballendine and the Reverend John McKay, seemingly lacked his command of the language, and his role soon grew well beyond the chiefs' side.
entries.source_note: Erasmus, Buffalo Days and Nights (1976), via DCB (Payne) and Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan (Cottrell); exact day not established

entries.headline: The first council, and a request to adjourn
entries.digest: Jackes's narrative of the proceedings opens with this first council: the Cree ceremony of reception, then Morris's address. When he finished, the chiefs asked for an adjournment to consider what they had heard among themselves.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition): Jackes's narrative

entries.headline: The Queen's promise, as long as the sun shines
entries.digest: In his opening address Morris spoke for the Queen and promised that what was agreed would endure. He gave no detailed terms that day, only the frame and the promise of permanence.
entries.quote: as long as that sun shines and yonder river flows
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition): Jackes's narrative

entries.headline: Terms laid out: reserves, money, implements
entries.digest: Morris set out the offer: reserves of one square mile for each family of five, a present of twelve dollars a head, five dollars a year forever, more for chiefs and headmen, ammunition and twine, schools, and tools and cattle for those who farmed. He insisted the same offer had been accepted elsewhere.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Mistawāsis asks for time to think quietly
entries.digest: Presented as head chief, Mistawāsis asked that the people be given time. In the interpreter's English he said a matter thought over quietly was best decided. Jackes records the council adjourning on that request.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition): Jackes's narrative

entries.headline: A Duck Lake messenger asks for the terms in advance
entries.digest: A messenger from Beardy's people came to ask what the terms would be before they agreed to come. Morris refused to give them separately. Jackes notes it as an interruption; it was the start of a second negotiation.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: This is our land, not a piece of pemmican
entries.digest: After the reserve offer, Poundmaker answered that the land was already theirs and they would take what they wanted. Erasmus remembered him saying it was not a piece of pemmican to be cut up and handed back in pieces, and the seated people shouting approval until the head chiefs restored order. The line is not in the commission's record.
entries.source_note: Erasmus, Buffalo Days and Nights (1976), as summarised in The Canadian Encyclopedia (2016) and Manitoba Education BLM 6.1.4c; day not stated

entries.headline: Sunday services at the fort and in the camp
entries.digest: No council sat. Services were held at the fort and in the Cree camp, with the Reverend John McKay among the clergy. Jackes records the day as a pause; in the lodges the argument went on.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Inside the chiefs' council: Mistawāsis carries the doubters
entries.digest: Erasmus sat in the chiefs' own deliberations. Poundmaker and The Badger spoke strongly against signing. Mistawāsis answered them, and Ahtahkakoop followed in support; Erasmus credits Mistawāsis's speech with persuading the reluctant leaders. In his telling the two head chiefs, not the commissioners, settled the matter.
entries.source_note: Erasmus, Buffalo Days and Nights (1976), via DCB and Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan; date inferred from the adjournments

entries.headline: Head chiefs ask for one more day
entries.digest: The head chiefs came to say they had not finished deliberating and needed another day. Morris agreed. Jackes's narrative is brief; the record of what was decided that day lies in the chiefs' council, not his.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: How will I clothe and feed my children?
entries.digest: Poundmaker asked for help in the hard years of settling, for those to come as well as for themselves, and begged the commissioners to assist in every way. He said that from what he heard he could not see how the offer would feed and clothe his children. Morris replied that the Crown could not feed the whole people every day.
entries.quote: I cannot understand that I shall be able to clothe my children (as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative in Morris (1880); quoted in DCB (Dempsey). Sources differ on whether the line falls on 22 or 23 Aug

entries.headline: Food in the spring when we begin to farm
entries.digest: Ahtahkakoop asked for food at the planting seasons, when the people would be breaking land instead of hunting. His request was specific and seasonal: not rations forever, but help to get through the change.
entries.quote: We want food in the spring when we commence to farm (as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 22 Aug, in Morris (1880); AccessGenealogy transcription

entries.headline: Not food every day, but at the start and in famine
entries.digest: Mistawāsis narrowed the demand to answer Morris's objection. They did not ask to be fed every day, he said, only when they began to farm and in case of famine. This was the wording the famine clause would grow from.
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 22 Aug, in Morris (1880)

entries.headline: Famine is a special case; daily rations refused
entries.digest: Morris said the government could not support the people from day to day. A great sickness or famine, he allowed, stood as a special case. He promised to consider the requests overnight.
entries.quote: Some great sickness or famine stands as a special case
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 22 Aug, in Morris (1880)

entries.headline: McKay: we have not come to deceive you
entries.digest: McKay spoke to the chiefs directly. The commissioners had not come to cheat them, he said, but they could not promise to feed everyone daily. He spoke as a Cree-speaking Métis, not through an interpreter.
entries.quote: We have not come here to deceive you (as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 22 Aug, in Morris (1880)

entries.headline: The Badger: think of our children
entries.digest: Jackes records The Badger, who had opposed the treaty in the chiefs' council, now asking for help once families settled on reserves rather than daily feeding. He said they must think of their children and did not want to be too greedy.
entries.quote: we do not want to be too greedy (The Badger, as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 22 Aug, in Morris (1880)

entries.headline: Erasmus reads out the chiefs' list of demands
entries.digest: When the council resumed, Erasmus read the list the chiefs had agreed: more cattle and implements, provisions while they settled, help in famine, a free supply of medicines, missionaries and schools, and other items. Jackes's narrative names him as the reader, which confirms his central place.
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 23 Aug, in Morris (1880); AccessGenealogy transcription

entries.headline: Medicine chest, famine aid and three years of provisions
entries.digest: Morris refused open-ended food but granted more cattle and tools, a thousand dollars a year for three years for provisions at seeding time for bands that farmed, help in a general famine or pestilence, and a medicine chest at each agent's house. None of these was in Treaties 1 to 5.
entries.quote: medicine chest will be kept at the house of each Indian agent
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 23 Aug, in Morris (1880); The Canadian Encyclopedia (2016)

entries.headline: A show of hands; Ahtahkakoop signs
entries.digest: Ahtahkakoop asked the people to show whether they agreed, and Jackes records shouts and raised hands. He and Mistawāsis then signed after the commissioners, followed by the other chiefs and councillors, Poundmaker among them.
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 23 Aug, in Morris (1880); Ahtahkakoop First Nation entry (USask)

entries.headline: Joseph Thoma's late demands, disowned
entries.digest: Before the signing, Joseph Thoma, speaking for Red Pheasant's people, said the offer was too little and asked for more, including ten miles of land around the reserves. Red Pheasant disowned him. Jackes records the demands only in summary.
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 23 Aug, in Morris (1880)

entries.headline: Medals, flags, and the counting begins
entries.digest: On the 24th the chiefs received medals, uniforms and flags, and payments began. Christie's count for Carlton came to 13 chiefs, 44 headmen, 262 men, 473 women, 473 boys and 481 girls, with 41 people from Treaty 4: 1,787 in all.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Beardy wants his words written down
entries.digest: At the separate meeting, Beardy and his councillor Say-sway-kus said they were anxious about the vanishing buffalo and asked for a law to protect them. Beardy asked that his request be written. Morris said the North-West Council would consider a buffalo law. Beardy signed, his biographer writes, because he saw no other course.
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 28 Aug, in Morris (1880); DCB, Kamīyistowesit

entries.headline: The Willow Cree are paid at McKay's camp
entries.digest: The Duck Lake council met at McKay's camp rather than the Carlton ground, satisfying Beardy's refusal without moving the treaty. When the Willow Cree accepted, they were paid there. Their signatures were added to the same treaty document under the date 28 August.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880); LAC IT 296 (signed 23 and 28 Aug)

entries.headline: Accounts settled at Carlton
entries.digest: Christie closed the Carlton accounts. Over the whole journey the commission drew on a sixty-thousand-dollar credit and later returned $12,730.55 unspent to the Receiver General. On the 31st he and Morris left for Fort Pitt.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Arrival at Fort Pitt
entries.digest: After a week on the trail west along the North Saskatchewan, Morris and Christie reached Fort Pitt, where the Cree of the western plains were gathering.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Sweet Grass arrives and greets the governor
entries.digest: Sweet Grass came in and greeted the commissioners warmly, the man who had asked for this council five years before. Jackes records the welcome rather than any terms.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Pipe dance, then Morris's address
entries.digest: After the pipe dance, Morris addressed the Fort Pitt Cree with the same offer as at Carlton, telling them of the road ahead and the Queen's aims. The next day, 8 September, the people asked for more time, as Carlton had.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Sweet Grass accepts and signs first
entries.digest: Sweet Grass accepted the terms, taking the governor's hand to his heart, and prayed that there be no more bloodshed between white and red. He was the first signatory at Fort Pitt; nine chiefs signed with their councillors.
entries.quote: May the white man's blood never be spilt on this earth (as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition); DCB, Wikaskokiseyin

entries.headline: Erasmus interprets at Fort Pitt
entries.digest: Erasmus went on with the commission and interpreted the Fort Pitt talks, as he later did at the adhesions signed there in 1877. His presence carried the Carlton understanding west.
entries.source_note: DCB (Payne); day of his interpreting not specified

entries.headline: Big Bear arrives too late, and will not sign
entries.digest: Big Bear came in after the signing and payments. He said he had been sent by the Cree and Nakoda still hunting on the plains and could not sign without them. He asked the governor to spare him what he most dreaded, the rope about his neck. Sweet Grass and others urged him to sign; he did not.
entries.quote: the rope to be about my neck (as interpreted)
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 13 Sept, in Morris (1880); DCB, Mistahimaskwa

entries.headline: Morris answers: the law will hang murderers
entries.digest: Morris took Big Bear's words literally. The Queen's law punished murder with death, he replied, and no treaty could change it. He restated the famine clause as help only if a great famine or pestilence fell on the whole people, not on single bands. He left that afternoon for Battle River; Big Bear's biographer notes that Morris judged him a coward.
entries.quote: a great famine or pestilence upon the whole Indian people
entries.source_note: Jackes's narrative, 13 Sept, in Morris (1880); DCB, Mistahimaskwa

entries.headline: Morris reports the treaties to Ottawa
entries.digest: Back at Fort Garry since 6 October, Morris wrote his formal report to the Minister of the Interior. He explained the journey, the reasons for the treaties and the terms added at Carlton, and made recommendations on preserving the buffalo, on the Métis, and on teachers for the reserves.
entries.source_note: Morris (1880), ch. IX (UVic Confederation edition)

entries.headline: Big Bear refuses again before Laird
entries.digest: At Sounding Lake Big Bear met Lieutenant Governor David Laird and still would neither sign nor take presents, so no reserve could be set aside for him. His refusal stopped survey work near Medicine Hat that autumn.
entries.source_note: DCB, Mistahimaskwa (month given, day not)

entries.headline: Hunger brings Big Bear's adhesion
entries.digest: With the buffalo gone and his people reduced to fishing and gophers, Big Bear signed an adhesion to Treaty 6 at Fort Walsh so that the police would feed his band. His following then numbered 247. He had held out six years.
entries.source_note: DCB, Mistahimaskwa

entries.headline: The Herald: a treaty is a contract to farm
entries.digest: The day after Big Bear signed at Fort Walsh, the Herald argued that the treaties were a contract obliging the nations to use the tools and supplies provided. It blamed the people's slowness to change their way of life for their want.
entries.source_note: Herald, 9 Dec 1882, as cited in Hildebrandt (1978)

entries.headline: The Herald mocks Big Bear's road to Ottawa
entries.digest: Big Bear now wanted to deal with no one but the head of the Indian Department in Ottawa. The Herald ridiculed the demand. His biographer reports that he would deal with no one below the head of the Indian Department.
entries.source_note: Herald, 8 Mar 1884, as cited in Hildebrandt (1978); DCB, Mistahimaskwa

entries.headline: Elders: the medicine chest meant doctors and hospitals
entries.digest: Interviewed by Lynn Hickey, Alberta Treaty 6 Elders said the promise was doctors, medicines and hospitals, symbolised by the medicine chest, and that Treaty people were not to pay for medical care. They said this promise had been broken. Their account is oral history handed down a century after the council.
entries.source_note: Hickey (1976), as summarised in Craft and Lebihan, NCCIH (2021)

entries.place: Treaty 6 and other treaty communities, Saskatchewan
entries.headline: Elders: the land shared to the depth of a plough
entries.digest: Elders recorded for 'Treaty Elders of Saskatchewan' said the land was to be shared with the newcomers, not surrendered: the settlers could use it to the depth of a plough blade, but it was not sold or given away. They called the relationship wîtaskêwin, living together on the land. The written treaty's cession clause states a surrender.
entries.source_note: Cardinal and Hildebrandt (2000), as cited in OTC, Treaty Implementation (2007), pp. 18–19

entries.headline: The manuscript treaty comes back to Carlton
entries.digest: For the 150th anniversary the ten-page original manuscript was shown inside the walls of Fort Carlton, brought back by Chief Edwin Ananas of Beardy's and Okemasis' Cree Nation, with further showings planned at Beardy's campsite and Fort Pitt. Speakers described the treaty's spirit and intent as two peoples living off the land together, and said some treaty rights were still being secured.
entries.source_note: Allison Bamford, CP24/CTV News, 22 Aug 2026

claims.claim: Presents are bait in a fox-trap; Big Bear wants none of them
claims.evidence: George McDougall's report of 23 Oct 1875, in Morris (1880)

claims.claim: Mistawāsis welcomes the coming treaty: that is all we wanted
What is agreed will last as long as the sun shines and the river flows
Offer: one square mile per family of five, $12 present, $5 a year, ammunition, twine, tools, schools
The land is ours, not a piece of pemmican to be cut up and handed back
claims.evidence: Erasmus, Buffalo Days and Nights (memoir, 1976); not in the commission's record

claims.claim: Not food every day, only when we begin to farm and in case of famine
No daily rations; a great sickness or famine is a special case
Chiefs' list read out: cattle, implements, provisions, famine help, free medicines, schools
Treaty text: a medicine chest at each Indian agent's house, at the agent's direction
claims.evidence: Treaty No. 6 (LAC IT 296); quoted by PLEA Saskatchewan

claims.claim: Treaty text: aid if the people are overtaken by pestilence or general famine; $1,000 a year for three years at seeding
Protect the remaining buffalo, and write the request down
Accepts the terms and signs first at Fort Pitt, praying for no bloodshed
Will not sign without the plains camps; asks to be spared the rope about his neck
Signs an adhesion to Treaty 6 at Fort Walsh so his band will be fed
claims.evidence: DCB, Mistahimaskwa; LAC lists the Treaty 6 adhesions

claims.claim: The medicine chest meant doctors, medicines and hospitals, free of charge
claims.evidence: Hickey (1976), via Craft and Lebihan, NCCIH (2021)

claims.claim: Land was shared to the depth of a plough, never surrendered

convergences.label: The first council at Carlton
convergences.note: Morris speaks of a promise as lasting as the sun; Jackes records the pipe-stem and the adjournment; Erasmus, newly hired by the chiefs, is the one man who will hear both what was said in English and what the Cree heard.

convergences.label: The offer is put, and answered
convergences.note: Morris states his terms as settled; Mistawāsis asks for quiet thought; Poundmaker's angry answer survives only in Erasmus's memory, not in Jackes's minutes.

convergences.label: The chiefs' council behind the public one
convergences.note: Jackes records a Sunday of services; Erasmus, inside the lodges, records the decisive argument. The same weekend appears as a pause in one record and the turning point in the other.

convergences.label: Food, famine and children
convergences.note: The hardest day: Cree speakers ask for help in settling, in spring and in famine; Morris refuses daily rations but calls famine a special case; McKay insists no deceit is meant. The famine clause is born in this exchange.

convergences.label: Requests read, clauses granted, treaty signed
convergences.note: Erasmus reads the chiefs' list; Morris grants the medicine chest and famine aid; Ahtahkakoop calls for a show of hands. What was asked, what was said aloud and what was written are three slightly different things.

convergences.label: Duck Lake signs on its own ground
convergences.note: Beardy will not come to Carlton, so the commission comes to him; he asks for the buffalo to be protected and gets a promise of consideration, not a clause.

convergences.label: Fort Pitt accepts
convergences.note: Sweet Grass, who asked for a treaty in 1871, signs first and speaks of peace; four days later Big Bear arrives to refuse.

convergences.label: The rope about the neck
convergences.note: Big Bear asks to be spared the rope; Morris answers about hanging for murder. Whether the words meant a gallows, a lost freedom, or both is still argued.

convergences.label: Big Bear signs; Battleford comments
convergences.note: Big Bear signs at Fort Walsh to feed his people; the next day the Herald at Battleford tells its readers the treaty is a contract to farm.

ties.note: Mistawāsis and Ahtahkakoop hired Erasmus as their own interpreter at Carlton; he credits Mistawāsis's speech with carrying the council.
Ahtahkakoop jointly engaged Erasmus; both supported the treaty.
Erasmus, who favoured the treaty, is the sole source for Poundmaker's pemmican objection in the chiefs' council.
The chiefs' interpreter was later paid by the commission too, which brought him charges of divided loyalty.
Jackes's narrative is printed inside Morris's 1880 book: the secretary's record became the commissioner's case.
Allied head chiefs who led acceptance together at Carlton and signed side by side on 23 August.
Morris read the rope as fear of the gallows and thought Big Bear a coward; Big Bear held out six years.
McDougall's 1875 portrait of Big Bear as a troublemaker preceded him to Fort Pitt.
McDougall carried the governor's message to Mistawāsis in 1875 and reported his welcome.
Sweet Grass urged Big Bear to sign at Fort Pitt on 13 September and came with him to bid Morris farewell.
McKay met Beardy before the council and hosted the Duck Lake signing at his camp.
Both doubted the terms in 1876; after 1885 both were convicted and photographed together as prisoners at Regina and Stony Mountain.
The Battleford paper followed Big Bear's refusals and mocked his demand to treat in Ottawa.
The Elders' accounts of a shared land and full medical care sit beside Morris's written text of cession and a medicine chest at the agent's direction.

threads_out.note: The same northern Plains buffalo economy underlies both councils, and Nakoda (Assiniboine) people took part in both: at Horse Creek with the United States, and in Canada among the bands that took Treaty 6. Morris's warning that the herds were vanishing was the fear Crazy Bear voiced a quarter century earlier.

Like Treaty 6, the Medicine Lodge treaties promised clothing, implements and farm instruction to buffalo nations as the herds collapsed; Big Bear's camp followed the last herds south into Montana in 1879.

Both are Crown treaties whose meaning is still argued between the written English text and what the nations understood from the spoken council: cession or sharing, a medicine chest or a right to health.

images.title: Treaty 6, manuscript original (IT 296)
images.caption: Library and Archives Canada's manuscript original, signed at Fort Carlton on 23 and 28 August and at Fort Pitt on 9 September 1876. It is the only numbered treaty whose written text includes a medicine chest and a pestilence-and-famine clause. In August 2026 it returned to Fort Carlton for the 150th anniversary.

images.title: Copy of Treaty No. 6 (printed)
images.caption: A contemporary printed copy of the treaty 'between Her Majesty the Queen and the Plain and Wood Cree Indians and other tribes' at Fort Carlton, Fort Pitt and Battle River: the government's version as circulated in print.
images.credit: Canadiana (Canadian Institute for Historical Microreproductions, no. 39206)

images.title: Cree Chief Big Bear, 1885
images.caption: Oliver Buell's portrait of Mistahi-maskwa in leg irons after his surrender in 1885. It was taken nine years after he asked Morris to spare him the rope, and was made for sale to eastern buyers.
images.credit: Oliver Buell; Library and Archives Canada, C-001873

images.title: Big Bear, Poundmaker and others at Regina, 1885
images.caption: Group photograph taken during the 1885 trials at Regina, with Big Bear and Poundmaker seated in the front row. Both men had spoken against the terms in 1876.
images.credit: Oliver Buell; Library and Archives Canada, C-001872

images.title: Prisoners at Stony Mountain Penitentiary, 1886
images.caption: Big Bear and Poundmaker with Father Albert Lacombe, the warden Sam Bedson and other clergy at Stony Mountain, Manitoba. Both chiefs were released in poor health and died soon after: Poundmaker in 1886, Big Bear in 1888.
images.credit: Unknown photographer; Glenbow Archives, University of Calgary, NA-20-2
